extracted.intended_audience: patent applicants, patent attorneys, and patent examiners (JPO/CNIPA-focused)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and worked examples for assessing patent applications (inventive step, eligibility, enablement/support) primarily under JPO and CNIPA practice, including how to compare claims to cited prior art and evaluate machine-learning/software-related inventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Difference identification between claim and cited document
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify specific points at which the invention of Claim 1 and the cited invention differ (e.g., presence of front-and-rear and left-right fuzzy decision-making systems and the specific steps (1)～(6)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: List the concrete technical feature(s) that are not specified in the cited document. The examiner's analysis compares the claim's steps/features with those disclosed in D1 and explicitly states the 'Difference' before evaluating its significance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inventive step — could person skilled in the art easily conceive?
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess whether, in view of the closest prior art and common general technical knowledge, a person skilled in the art could have easily conceived the claimed invention (i.e., whether the claimed solution is obvious).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider whether prior art suggests the technical matters in the difference; check if differences would be mere design variations or routine choices. If no suggestion exists and an advantageous effect is shown, conclude inventive step (JPO/CNIPA examples). Conversely, if prior art gives motivation to replace or combine techniques, conclude lack of inventive step.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presence of advantageous technical effect supporting inventive step
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether the claimed differences yield an advantageous effect (e.g., improved reliability and accuracy of stability/fall-direction judgment; improved operational efficiency of hardware).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain how the effect is produced (e.g., fusion of sensors + fuzzy algorithm yields better judgment; padding weight parameters to target sizes improves hardware efficiency). Use demonstrated/argued effects to support non-obviousness when prior art lacks such effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Absence of prior-art suggestion / not a design variation
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate whether there is any basis in cited documents to assume the claimed technical matter is a mere 'design variation' or routine design choice from the prior art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If no prior art suggests the specific algorithmic or structural feature and it is not common general knowledge, treat it as non-trivial. Examiners explicitly state when 'there is also no basis for assuming that the technical matter in question is "design variation, etc." from the cited document.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Functional interaction between algorithmic features and technical features
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess whether algorithmic features (e.g., fuzzy decision/ML algorithm, parameter-adjusting algorithms) functionally support and interact with the technical features of the apparatus/system, thereby producing a technical effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: CNIPA: if algorithmic features 'functionally support each other and have an interaction relationship with the technical features,' that supports inventive step. Examiners look for functional coupling, not mere abstract computation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obviousness by combination of references (motivation to combine)
rubrics_metrics.description: Decide whether combining multiple cited documents would make the claimed invention obvious, i.e., whether there exists technical motivation to combine D1 and D2 (or others) to arrive at the claimed solution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If references disclose complementary teachings and provide a technical motivation to combine them (e.g., D2 teaches Messy GA can solve drawbacks of CGA and D1 uses GA for path planning), examiners may conclude lack of inventive step. Evaluate whether the combination would produce expected effects without undue experimentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assessment of obstructive factors
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider whether any non-obvious 'obstructive factor' exists that would prevent a skilled person from applying prior-art teaching to reach the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners note absence of obstructive factors as supporting obviousness; presence of obstructive factors or unexpected technical difficulty supports inventive step.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subject-matter eligibility for software-related inventions (JPA Article 29(1) analysis)
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether claimed information processing is implemented by specific means (co-operation of software and hardware) such that the claimed apparatus constitutes a technical creation utilizing a law of nature and thus falls under 'invention'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for recited concrete means (storage means, reception means, simulation and output means, etc.) and whether software processing is specifically implemented using hardware resources. If so, conclude the claim is technical (JPO example: business plan design apparatus).

rubrics_metrics.name: Enablement / sufficiency of disclosure (Article 36(4)(i) / 36(6)(i))
rubrics_metrics.description: Decide whether the description discloses the invention such that a person skilled in the art can make and use the invention (e.g., can generate the claimed estimation model using a generally used ML algorithm and appropriate training data).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if precise correlations are not shown, examiners may accept that common general technical knowledge permits a skilled person to obtain the estimation model. Check that inputs/outputs, training-data types, and implementation modes are described sufficiently for reproduction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reliance on common general technical knowledge to fill gaps
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate whether missing specifics in the description (e.g., explicit correlation between web advertisement/mention data and sales quantity) can be reasonably presumed from common general technical knowledge at the filing date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If such presumptions are reasonable (e.g., known correlations or known ML training procedures), the disclosure may be treated as sufficient. Examiners explicitly state when they rely on common general technical knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims supported by the description (support requirement)
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess whether the claims are supported by the detailed description and do not extend beyond what the description discloses (i.e., whether the skilled person can obtain the claimed technical solution from the description).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners check that the claimed technical solution is derivable from the description and that the description 'sets forth the invention in a manner sufficiently clear and complete' to satisfy statutory support provisions (CNIPA/JPA examples).

rubrics_metrics.name: Concrete implementation of functional claim elements
rubrics_metrics.description: When claims recite functional modules (e.g., 'model generation means', 'feature value obtainment means'), determine whether the description provides sufficient concrete implementation (algorithms, data types, processing steps) to carry out those functions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners accepted claims where the description explained what web advertisement data and mention data are, how mention evaluation values can be obtained, and that general ML algorithms (neural networks) with training data can generate the model. Lack of concrete implementation may risk insufficiency.
